newsitem.title: USA: U.S. dismisses charge of violating Iraq-Kuwait DMZ.
newsitem.headline: U.S. dismisses charge of violating Iraq-Kuwait DMZ.

text.p: A U.S. spokesman dismissed as "absolutely absurd" charges by a U.N. officer that U.S. missile attacks on Iraq and overflights on Wednesday by unidentified warplanes violated an Iraq-Kuwait demilitarized zone.

Maj.-Gen. Gian Santillo, Force Commander of the U.N. Iraq-Kuwait Observer Mission (UNIKOM), told Reuters two warplanes seen circling over the border had broken the terms of the U.N.-mandated zone set up after the Gulf War.

He added that UNIKOM observers had seen some of the 44 U.S. cruise missiles fired at targets in southern Iraq on Sept. 3 and 4 fly over the zone. UNIKOM had reported both sightings to U.N. headquarters in New York, he said.
"I saw that report. It's absolutely absurd," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told journalists.

U.S., British and French warplanes fly from Saudi Arabia to enforce a no-fly-zone over southern Iraq imposed after the 1991 Gulf War. They also patrol another no-fly-zone over northern Iraq from a base in Turkey.

"These no-flight-zones were not set up through U.N. resolutions, but they were set up consistent with U.N. resolutions and certainly consistent with the state of the world as it was in 1991," Burns said.
"It still makes sense and we're going to continue, no matter what any of these officials say."
Western diplomats said they did not expect a diplomatic incident over the UNIKOM report, saying it was a "theoretical" matter that had not been an issue at U.N. headquarters.
